claim_verdicts.evidence: RFC 9110 §3.3: "HTTP is defined as a stateless protocol, meaning that each request message's semantics can be understood in isolation, and that the relationship between connections and messages on them has no impact on the interpretation of those messages." Abstract: "The Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) is a stateless application-level protocol". Both halves of the claim sit in that §3.3 sentence.

RFC 9110 §3.3: "the relationship between connections and messages on them has no impact on the interpretation of those messages", then "Many implementations depend on HTTP's stateless design in order to reuse proxied connections or dynamically load balance requests across multiple servers." §11.1 adds: "HTTP authentication is presumed to be stateless: all of the information necessary to authenticate a request MUST be provided in the request, rather than be dependent on the server remembering prior requests."

RFC 6265 §4.1: "The Set-Cookie HTTP response header is used to send cookies from the server to the user agent." §4.2.1: "The user agent sends stored cookies to the origin server in the Cookie header." §3.1 shows the round trip: "== Server -> User Agent == Set-Cookie: SID=31d4d96e407aad42" then "== User Agent -> Server == Cookie: SID=31d4d96e407aad42". Direction and header names are exactly as claimed.

RFC 6265 §4.1.1 grammar: "set-cookie-string = cookie-pair *( \";\" SP cookie-av )" — one cookie-pair per Set-Cookie, the rest are attributes; also "Origin servers SHOULD NOT fold multiple Set-Cookie header fields into a single header field." §4.2.1: "cookie-string = cookie-pair *( \";\" SP cookie-pair )", as in the §3.1 example "Cookie: SID=31d4d96e407aad42; lang=en-US". §5.4: "the user agent MUST NOT attach more than one Cookie header field."

RFC 6265 §5.4: "The user agent includes stored cookies in the Cookie HTTP request header" and "A user agent MAY omit the Cookie header in its entirety." Its algorithm keys on the cookie's own fields: "The cookie's host-only-flag is true and the canonicalized request-host is identical to the cookie's domain"; "The request-uri's path path-matches the cookie's path"; a true secure-only-flag requires a "secure" scheme. §4.1.2.3: "If the server omits the Domain attribute, the user agent will return the cookie only to the origin server" — the lab sets no Domain, so host-only applies.

RFC 6265 §4.1.2.4: "The scope of each cookie is limited to a set of paths, controlled by the Path attribute"; "The user agent will include the cookie in an HTTP request only if the path portion of the request-uri matches (or is a subdirectory of) the cookie's Path attribute". §5.1.4 path-match: "The cookie-path is a prefix of the request-path, and the last character of the cookie-path is %x2F (\"/\")" — with cookie-path "/" that holds for every request-path.

RFC 6265 §4.1.2.6: "The HttpOnly attribute limits the scope of the cookie to HTTP requests. In particular, the attribute instructs the user agent to omit the cookie when providing access to cookies via 'non-HTTP' APIs (such as a web browser API that exposes cookies to scripts)." Both halves of the claim — withhold from non-HTTP interfaces, and that is what stops page scripts reading it — are in that sentence.

RFC 6265 §4.1.2.5: "the user agent will include the cookie in an HTTP request only if the request is transmitted over a secure channel (typically HTTP over Transport Layer Security (TLS))", and "secure" is "defined by the user agent" — so "a connection it considers secure" is the right wording. §8.3: "Unless sent over a secure channel (such as TLS), the information in the Cookie and Set-Cookie headers is transmitted in the clear" and is "exposed to an eavesdropper." §4.1.2.6 gives HttpOnly no confidentiality on the wire.

No admissible source exists here. Grep for "SameSite|samesite" over refs/rfc/rfc6265.txt returns 0 matches; the attribute is absent from every mirrored RFC. content/versions.yaml has no cookie key — standards.http points at RFC 9110, which defines no cookie header — so no docs root there covers SameSite either. It is specified only in draft-ietf-httpbis-rfc6265bis, not mirrored and not a published RFC. Kind is behavior, so this does not block; open since round 1.

RFC 6265 §8.4: "servers commonly store a nonce (or 'session identifier') in a cookie. When the server receives an HTTP request with a nonce, the server can look up state information associated with the cookie using the nonce as a key." And: "Using session identifier cookies limits the damage an attacker can cause if the attacker learns the contents of a cookie because the nonce is useful only for interacting with the server" — the "means nothing outside the server that issued it" and "worth what the state is worth" halves.

Caddyfile at stage-0, inside the plain-HTTP site block ":8080": "handle /login.html { header Set-Cookie \"sid=dev-session-1; Path=/; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax\" file_server }". The only TLS site is "donhang.local:8443 { tls internal ... }", which serves files and sets no cookie. Recorded capture line 5 is character-for-character "Set-Cookie: sid=dev-session-1; Path=/; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax". The string "Secure" occurs nowhere in the Caddyfile.

Caddyfile: "@guest header Cookie *role=guest*", "@signedIn header Cookie *sid=*", then handle /admin { route { respond @guest ... 403; respond @signedIn ... 200; respond ... 401 } }. Substring matching, and that nothing is filed, are right. But @guest is written and evaluated first inside route, so a Cookie line holding both sid= and role=guest answers 403, not the 200 the claim's second case promises: three overlapping cases, no precedence named. Still unfixed in .meta.json.
claim_verdicts.suggested_text: At tag stage-0 /admin answers 403 for any Cookie line containing role=guest (that test runs first), 200 for a Cookie line containing sid= and not role=guest, and 401 otherwise, including when no Cookie header is sent; both tests are substring matches on the header, so the lab keeps no state behind the value.

claim_verdicts.evidence: curl is not a versions.yaml key and is not mirrored, and Docker is not runnable here, so the evidence is the recorded run. The script rm -f's "$jar" (line 8); step 2's -c recreates it and step 3 finds "sid dev-session-1" in it; step 4 differs from step 1 only by -b and turns 401 into 200 — so -c saves and -b sends back. With -o /dev/null step 1 prints "   401" alone, without the Caddyfile's 401 body text, while step 2's headers still reach grep via -D -. No progress meter appears, though lab-run.sh merges stderr into stdout.

Recorded execution. cookie-roundtrip.sh line 28 runs curl with -H 'Cookie: role=guest' and no jar option; capture line 14 prints 403. Caddy reaches 403 only through the matcher "@guest header Cookie *role=guest*", which tests a request header — so what -H wrote did arrive as one. The server never sets role=guest: the only Set-Cookie in the Caddyfile is sid=dev-session-1, and the jar written in step 2 holds only sid.

The 403 half is exact — RFC 9110 §15.5.4: "The 403 (Forbidden) status code indicates that the server understood the request but refuses to fulfill it." The 401 half is broader than §15.5.2, which ties 401 to the authentication framework: the request "lacks valid authentication credentials for the target resource. The server generating a 401 response MUST send a WWW-Authenticate header field ... containing at least one challenge". A missing cookie is not credentials in that sense, and the lab sends no challenge, so the claim's flat rule is wider than the text.
claim_verdicts.suggested_text: In this lab 401 is the answer when the request carries nothing the server accepts as identity; RFC 9110 defines 401 for requests lacking valid authentication credentials and requires a WWW-Authenticate challenge, which this lab does not send. 403 says the server understood the request and refuses it; here that is any Cookie line containing role=guest. Other Cookie lines answer 401.

claim_verdicts.evidence: Capture line 8 is "#HttpOnly_localhost FALSE / FALSE 0 sid dev-session-1". The script rm -f's $jar and only step 2's `curl -c "$jar"` recreates it, so the line is the client's own record. The host localhost and the path / are both there, three further fields are curl's bookkeeping (they interleave rather than following host and path in a block), and the last two fields are the name sid and the value dev-session-1, nothing personal anywhere. The only order the claim asserts — name and value last — is correct.

True of cookies the client stores and resends by itself: RFC 6265 §5.4 puts every such decision in the user agent's algorithm, keyed on the stored attributes (domain-match, path-match, secure-only-flag, http-only-flag). As an absolute it is refuted by this lesson's own step 5, where -H 'Cookie: role=guest' has the code write a Cookie header by hand and the server acts on it: attributes constrain the automatic resend, not what a client may put in a request. The lesson text carries the condition; only the ledger overstates.
claim_verdicts.suggested_text: For a cookie the client stores and resends on its own, the attributes on Set-Cookie — not the application code writing the request — decide who may read the value and when it travels; a client can still write a Cookie header by hand, as step 5 of the script does.

claim_verdicts.evidence: www/login.html at stage-0 is 13 lines: doctype, head with title, then an h1 "Đăng nhập" and two paragraphs. No <form>, no <input>, no <script>. The header comes from the server configuration instead: "handle /login.html { header Set-Cookie \"sid=dev-session-1; ...\" file_server }", so any GET of the page receives it — which is what capture line 5 shows for a plain curl of /login.html.

No POSIX or GNU manual is mirrored and neither grep nor tr is a versions.yaml key, so this rests on the recorded run. Step 2 pipes the full header block of a Caddy 200 through `grep -i '^set-cookie:'` and the capture shows one line only — status line, Server, Date and Content-Type are gone. Step 3 reads the tab-separated cookie file through `tr '\t' ' '` and capture line 8 prints the seven fields separated by spaces, with no tabs left.

RFC 6761 is neither mirrored in refs/ nor a docs root in content/versions.yaml, so this rests on the repository. scripts/lab-run.sh line 18 runs every script inside the lab container (`docker compose exec -T lab ...`), and docker-compose.yml gives the web service `network_mode: "service:lab"` under the comment "8080 and 8443 belong to the web service, which shares this box's network so that localhost means the same thing in every lesson". So http://localhost:8080 from the script is that box's own port, and the capture shows the lab answering.
